annotations.title: Starlink satellites: Facts, tracking and impact on astronomy

content.text:
Assuming you mean **the first artificial satellite vs. modern “latest” satellites**:

| Feature | **First satellite: Sputnik 1** | **Latest/modern satellites** |
|---|---:|---:|
| Launch date | **October 4, 1957** | Constantly changing; new satellites launch almost every week |
| Country/operator | Soviet Union | Governments and companies worldwide |
| Size | About **58 cm / 23 in** diameter — like a beach ball | From shoebox-sized CubeSats to bus-sized spacecraft |
| Mass | **83.6 kg / 184 lb** | Can range from a few kg to several tons; modern Starlink V2 satellites are about **800 kg** each |
| Main purpose | Prove an object could orbit Earth; send simple radio “beeps” | Internet, GPS/navigation, weather, Earth imaging, military, science, communications |
| Technology | Battery-powered radio transmitter | Solar panels, computers, cameras/radar, electric propulsion, AI-assisted systems, laser links |
| Communication | Simple radio pulses | High-speed broadband, encrypted links, inter-satellite laser communication |
| Lifespan | About **3 months in orbit** before reentry | Often **5–15+ years**, depending on mission and orbit |
| Impact | Started the Space Age and Space Race | Supports daily life: maps, phones, banking time signals, weather forecasts, internet, climate monitoring |

**In short:** Sputnik 1 was a simple metal sphere that mainly proved orbital spaceflight was possible. Modern satellites are sophisticated robotic platforms that can image Earth, provide internet, guide navigation, monitor climate, and communicate globally.

Sputnik 1 was launched on **October 4, 1957**, weighed about **83.6 kg**, and orbited Earth about every **98 minutes**. ([history.nasa.gov](https://history.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/static/history/sputnik.html?utm_source=openai)) As of early June 2026, one very current example of modern satellite technology is SpaceX’s Starlink network, with over **10,000 satellites in orbit**, and its newer V2 satellites weighing about **800 kg** each. ([space.com](https://www.space.com/spacex-starlink-satellites.html?utm_source=openai))
